title: My tower defense roguelite game after 1 year of AI development from the very first line - Part 1
author: devtainer
selftext:
Hi Ai gang!

This is latest trailer of "Grumpy Hero Grinder" - a tower defense roguelite I've spent the past year building.

It’s about 99.9% vibe-coded. There were, however, slightly more than a couple of prompts involved.

AI helped me build major game systems in a couple of evenings. Getting to a prototype that my friends and I actually enjoyed playing took six months.

That gap is what I want to talk about in this first post.

Over the past year, I've used AI for coding, game design discussions, art, audio, marketing, analytics. I've found workflows that let me move surprisingly fast, made some costly mistakes, and nearly abandoned a game I and other people now enjoy playing.

I want to share my experience and hopefully, it'll save someone a few painful weeks :)

**My toolkit includes**: Unity + MCP, Claude Code, Codex, Blender + MCP, Meshy AI, Suno, and ElevenLabs.



**A little background**

\- matters here. I have a family, a full-time job, and over 13 years of professional SaaS software development experience. I've also been making games in Unity as a hobby for more than 10 years. My first projects were mobile games that did reasonably well.

Then came six years of attempts and failed projects as I tried to make my first PC game. Now I’m finally getting ready to release my first demo on Steam.

So although this game is almost entirely vibe-coded, I came into it with quite a bit of programming and Unity experience.



**The Beginning**

The project started as an experiment in late 2025, when I began playing around with the latest Claude Opus model. In three weeks, I built what I estimated would normally have taken me 2-3 months.

That was the moment I realised a true power of AI, and thought: okay, maybe I really can make a game of this size on my own in a year or two.

The original idea was simple: combine the defensive planning and trap combinations of Tower Defense with the progression and active combat of an Action Roguelite. The idea of a dungeon turning invading heroes into a “hero grinder” followed pretty naturally.

I wanted something approachable, with familiar dungeon traps and a boss who was fun to control.

My development process settled into three steps:

Discuss and refine the game design with ChatGPT, then write a design document describing the proposed mechanics and changes.

Give that document to Claude Opus and turn it into a technical implementation plan.

Work through the plan with Opus, implementing it step by step.

**TIP**: Keep context separated. One thing that helped - when working on game design, I kept the conversation only about the player’s experience and how the mechanics should work, no technical details. Technical implementation came afterward, in its own pass.



**Biggest Mistake**

This workflow let me move through substantial features very quickly. Since this was a prototype, I was comfortable leaving rough edges. The priority was to get something playable and find out whether the idea felt good.

And here's where I made my biggest mistake.

I’ll call it “AI ideation drift.” There may already be a name for it, but this is how it happened to me.

I spent a lot of time discussing ideas with AI: how mechanics could interact, how progression could work, what else we could add. At some point, I made a tiny change in direction without really noticing it. More decisions followed that change, and eventually I'd taken the game somewhere quite different from where I wanted to go.

The systems became increasingly focused on numbers, status effects, and interactions between them. I ended up with something much closer to a conventional tower defense game, where the dungeon boss felt like an extra thing to manage.

You could build towers, upgrade things, expand the map, and progress. It was a functioning, playable game.

I just didn't particularly want to play it. Neither did my friends.

The familiar dungeon traps I originally imagined didn't fit very well into the elaborate status-effect framework we'd designed. AI had helped me flesh out and implement those systems, and I'd kept investing in them because each individual piece seemed reasonable.

I'd lost track of the experience they were supposed to create.

There’s a video[ by awesome Jonas Tyroller](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s4k7yDfYx24) that captures the feeling of realizing you've drifted away from the game you wanted to make. It felt very familiar. Even experienced devs with great success do this mistake, and I feel it's extremly easy to do it with AI. Be carefull, don't let it drive you in a wrong direction.



**Recovery**

Stepping back was rough. These systems were connected, so changing direction meant reworking several of them together. I still couldn’t clearly see what the finished game should look like, and for a while I seriously considered abandoning the project.

Maybe the idea just didn’t work.

What helped me was realizing how far the prototype had moved from my original idea. I was ready to write off that idea based on a game that barely represented it anymore.

That original fantasy became something concrete to return to: defend your dungeon, combine recognizable traps, and enjoy smashing heroes yourself.

It took 4-5 very difficult weeks to rework the prototype into something I finally enjoyed playing. Remembering why I'd wanted to make it in the first place helped me get through that.

Another thing that helped was one of AI's biggest strengths: being able to try an idea quickly, even when you're not sure it deserves a place in the game.

At one point, I thought it might be fun if the boss could knock heroes out of the way simply by running into them.

I tried it, and it was fun. Physical knockback and knockdowns eventually became a core mechanic, with interactions across traps, items, perks and etc.

That little experiment helped me find the kind of game I'd wanted to make all along. It also reminded me to leave room for ideas that sound fun before I have a detailed explanation of how they fit into everything. I plan to share a full 9 months timelaps of development so you can see how those ideas evolved.



**Conclusions**

So yes: getting to a prototype that my friends and I enjoyed took roughly half a year, even with AI helping me implement large systems very quickly.

That was alongside a full-time job and family life, so your timeline may look very different. Especially if you avoid spending weeks enthusiastically developing the wrong things :)

The lesson I'm taking into the rest of the project is to keep checking the actual game against the experience I wanted to create. A productive evening can leave me with a working system and very little evidence that the game is more enjoyable.

I still need to play it, trust my own gut feel even more now. I need to give myself deadlines for experiments and be willing to change or discard things, even when they're already working.

AI has made it much easier for me to try ambitious ideas.

If there's interest, I could write more about what happened after the prototype: developing the visuals and "meat" of the game, generating 2D and 3D assets and audio, refining my workflow. I can also share how I use AI for marketing, along with some coding pitfalls and game dev tips. Yes, vibe coding still has those :)



For anyone else using AI to make games: have you experienced something similar, where individual design decisions seemed sensible but gradually pulled the project away from your original idea? How did you catch it?



P.S. If you’re curious about the game, [here's the recently updated Grumpy Hero Grinder Steam page](https://store.steampowered.com/app/5116620/Grumpy_Hero_Grinder/). A public demo is coming soon, and wishlists are very welcome :)



Thanks for reading! Hopefully, this helps someone avoid a few of my mistakes - or finally start making that game they’ve been thinking about.

comments.author: tema_msk
comments.body:
Looking good! Will wait for the next playtest. The “AI ideation drift” also got me. When you have ability to implement a, b, c features, that AI suggest, after whole day working on it, you can slip and agree with it. I compare it with motobike running uphill (no real experience, just the visualisation). You can go up very fast than by the foot. Faster than ever. But you need very carefully steer it, so you would not end up driving off the cliff.

Before it was more paced, like hiking speed. You have time to process and think and discuss your ideas with others.

comments.author: gpubattle
comments.body:
This is looking pretty polished. Taking more time on the project is definitely paying off.👍

For me, I been thinking that spanning out development over a long period of time while using AI to improve workflow is the move.

So I'm patient with my project. I'm using Trellis 2 for my 3d models and aggregating open source. But will look into paid work in the future for modeling.

What workflow are you using for your 3d models and assets?

replies.author: devtainer
replies.body:
Hey mate, I’m glad you liked it! I actually share the vision that good things take time. While it makes total sense to rush things a bit at the very beginning, everything from that initial phase up to the release should be treated more carefully. If you speed things up too much, you start losing a lot of quality - so I’d definitely prefer quality over quantity at this point.

Regarding 3D: 

I've purchased many asset packs from artists and adjusted them. 

When I need something unique, my process is: Ideation -> Sketching with ChatGPT images -> 3D generation in Meshy AI -> Blender MCP or manual updates -> Manual animations or searching. 

I have some basic Blender skills, so I can handle tasks like rigging and weight painting myself when it's tough, or ask AI when it's easy. 

I can also do animations, again, if no standard animation can be found. 

I use a bunch of self made AI skills that define the whole workflow of creating a model for the project, like handling common issues and visual styles. I can share more details in the next post if you find this topic interesting! 

Thanks for asking!

replies.author: gpubattle
replies.body:
This is something I will more interested in cause I realized that the quality of asset is key to then optimizing for performance but to still keep graphical quality. I going to have to look at the close sourced 3d generators and see the quality difference.

 Isn't they're a couple 3d generators, is Meshy AI the best? or is there alternatives that are just as good for certain things. I'm doing a FPS.

replies.author: devtainer
replies.body:
I don't want to sound like a meshy ad, but I am pretty happy with. I can't say it is the best, but there are few top projects and meshy pretty sure on of them. 

There are some tricks, as originally it doesn't do well for performance, so you need to do some postprocessing for each generation based on your own requirenments. FPS has more detailed graphics, so I can see your pain as I would not say that 3d generation is so good at the moment, so there might be some challenge in having models at the same moment of high quality and low on polygons for performance.

You can always adjust quality of the model with blender manually, just decreasing poly count and other things, it's easy.

So on your place I would use 3d generation at highest quality, but refining it with blender before adding to the game, as it gives you some crazy amounts 0.5-1 mln polys per 1 model which would kill any performance.
